title: The big questions heading into Nvidia's earnings amid a leadership crisis
excerpt: Nvidia is due to report their earnings days after the company's CEO Jensen Huang left in a shock departure — here's what you need to know.
content_html:
By Dan DeFrancesco

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

Executive Editor and lead writer for BI Today

2026-11-17T11:53:48.134Z

Has there ever been a more highly anticipated earnings call?

That's the question I keep asking myself ahead of Nvidia's earnings report, which drops after the bell today. As a millennial raised on NBC's "Must See TV" — look it up, youngsters — today's call has a similar feeling of appointment viewing.

But this isn't back-to-back episodes of "Friends" and "Seinfeld." The shocking departure of CEO Jensen Huang has left lots of unanswered questions. And that's on top of getting a financial update on the most important company to the AI trade.

We're going to be covering it all day on our live blog, but let's unpack the burning questions ahead of the big call:

Is it really so long, Huang? This past weekend saw the rise of the "Stand with Jensen" movement looking to get him reinstated. Two camps have emerged in Silicon Valley, with Bill Ackman laying out the strategy he'd use to bring back Huang. Jamie Heller, BI's editor in chief, even weighed in on the debate.

Nvidia's board of directors has reportedly closed that door. A person familiar with the matter told BI's Geoff Weiss the board is not considering reinstating Huang as CEO. Considering how many twists and turns this story has had, it's tough to take anything at face value.

And before you mention Sam Altman's ouster-turned-return at OpenAI, understand it's not an apples-to-apples comparison.

Still not convinced? BI's Peter Kafka explains why Nvidia has plenty of reasons not to bring back Huang.

If Huang is truly gone, when will Nvidia name a permanent CEO? Colette Kress, Nvidia's longtime CFO, stepped into the role on an interim basis. She could shake the tag, but she's not the favorite on prediction markets. That honor goes to two others: external candidate Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas and internal candidate Ian Buck, creator of Nvidia's all-important CUDA.

And it's not just a matter of who, but how long. With little-to-no succession plan and a flat org, Huang left his company in a deep hole that could take time to dig out of.

Is it still business as usual? It's not just that Huang's spent more than three decades building Nvidia. More recently, he's been strategic about expanding Nvidia beyond its GPU roots. That's come in the form of acquisitions, partnerships, and financing. In short, Nvidia has turned into a backstop for the entire AI industry.

Will it maintain the course, or change plans? It'll be tough for Kress to answer that in too much detail in her interim role. Judging by how all this shook out, it's safe to say some changes will come with the new CEO, though.

Speaking of business, how is that doing? Let's not forget this is still an earnings report. And one for a company that's a bellwether for the entire AI industry. Analysts have plenty of questions for executives outside Nvidia's leadership issues.

Unpacking financial guidance on the quarter and year ahead is high on the list. As is the impact the 2026 midterms, where voters largely came out against data centers, could have on Nvidia.

Then there's the Trump administration's recent decision to tighten access to advanced AI chips, which could represent another blow to Nvidia.

And now that Huang's gone, there's another AI company — one with a potential blockbuster IPO on Thursday — that stands to benefit, BI's Alistair Barr writes.

Dan DeFrancesco
